lines: A seven-channel precision adder: each row contributes either the signal patched into it or, with nothing patched, a steady voltage of its own, and the seven are added together at one output
Sets what its row contributes: with a cable in that row's jack it scales that signal from 0 to 1, and with the jack empty it is a steady 0V to 1V instead
Chooses the sign of its row, + adding it to the total and - subtracting it
Takes its row out of the total; the lamp lit means that row is muted
Holds the output at 0V whatever the seven rows are doing; the lamp lit means the module is muted
The signal for its row, scaled by that row's knob and then added to or subtracted from the total
The seven rows added together, one channel
Note — the module arrives silent. All seven row mutes and the overall mute come up switched on, so the output is held at 0V until those eight lamps are clicked off.
Note — a row with an empty jack contributes a steady voltage of 0V to 1V set by its knob, added or subtracted. That is what the module is for: seven unpatched rows can build a precise offset.
Note — the module is monophonic. Only the first channel of a polyphonic cable is read, and the output carries one channel.

Seven.notes: Source read at commit fcd92f3, the head of the repository and the only commit carrying the installed 2.0.0; its plugin.json is byte-identical to the installed one and all six res/ SVGs hash to the installed files. EVERY MUTE IS ON BY DEFAULT, SO THE MODULE IS SILENT WHEN IT IS PLACED. Adder.cpp:11 configures the seven row mutes with a default of 1.f and line 13 does the same for the overall mute, while process treats any value above 0 as muted (line 19 returns early, line 23 skips the row). The LedToggle SvgSwitch shows frame 1, the lit red lamp, at that value. The library screenshot shows them unlit because a widget with no module draws frame 0. The maker calls configParam with no name for any of the 22 parameters and calls neither configInput nor configOutput, so Rack shows an empty tooltip on every control and jack. The knobs and sign switches default to 1, which is a full level and a plus, so with the mutes off and nothing patched the output reads 7V.

lines: A clipper: the signal passes through untouched between two levels and is flattened at everything above and below them
Sets the level the signal is flattened at from above, -10V to 10V
Sets the level the signal is flattened at from below, -10V to 10V
Scales the HIGH CV input, 0 to 1, before that voltage is added to the HIGH knob
Scales the LOW CV input, 0 to 1, before that voltage is added to the LOW knob
Moves the upper flattening level, a volt per volt at the full HIGH CV setting, added to the HIGH knob
Moves the lower flattening level, a volt per volt at the full LOW CV setting, added to the LOW knob
The signal to be clipped
The input with everything above the upper level and below the lower level flattened to those levels
Note — the knobs come up at 10V and -10V, which is the whole range Rack uses, so the module passes a signal through unchanged until one of them is turned in.
Note — with the lower level set above the upper one the output rests at the lower level and the input is not heard at all.
Note — nothing limits a knob plus its CV, so either level can be driven well past 10V and stop clipping altogether.
Note — the module is monophonic. Only the first channel of a polyphonic cable is read, and the output carries one channel.

Cuter.notes: Source read at commit fcd92f3, settled the same way as SeVeN. rack::math::clamp takes the minimum against the upper bound first and the maximum against the lower bound second, so when the LOW knob is set above the HIGH knob the result is the LOW value and the input has no effect at all. The CV sums at Distortion.cpp:16 and 18 are not clamped, so a level can be pushed outside the -10V to 10V the knobs offer. No configParam names and no configInput or configOutput calls, so Rack shows an empty tooltip on every control and jack. The panel prints LOW, HIGH, LOW CV, HIGH CV, IN and OUT; the attenuating knob under each CV jack carries no label of its own.
